uncited: *   **Input:** A scene defined by a pre-generated Sparse Voxel Octree (STree) structure, camera position, and optional modification primitives (Union/Subtraction cubes).
**STree (Streaming Tree):** A low-level sparse octree contained within chunks of a high-level 2D uniform grid.
*   **Node Layout:** Each node (referred to as a "cell") represents a $64 \times 64 \times 64$ resolution voxel data block.
**GPU Voxel Pool:** A linear memory pool on the GPU.
*   **Page Layout:** Each streamed cell is allocated a new page.
**Visibility Buffer:** A 64-bit buffer used in the first rendering pass.
**Framebuffer:** A 64-bit buffer for the final result.
The CPU traverses the STree from the root cell to find the suitable level of detail (LOD).
If $LOD\_error > 0$, the CPU evaluates child cells, as the current cell does not meet the LOD metric.
A page is allocated in the voxel pool for this cell.
The voxelization result is written into a $64^3$ size buffer.
Voxels are rendered as points to the 64-bit visibility buffer.
The renderer reconstructs voxels from the visibility buffer using a method similar to Nanite [Karis et al. 2021].
Each compute thread reads one pixel from the visibility buffer to reconstruct the voxel as a geometry cube.
The voxel is rendered as a cube with 12 triangles.
**Selection:** A screen-pick operation retrieves the depth value from the framebuffer at the mouse click position $P$.
**Re-voxelization:** A voxelization shader is executed to re-voxelize the identified cells.
*   **Time Complexity:** The streaming phase depends on the tree traversal depth and the LOD metric evaluation.
The rendering phase is parallelized across compute threads, with each thread handling 64 voxels in Pass 1 and one pixel in Pass 2.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Linear storage in the GPU Voxel Pool.
The STree stores only existence flags, minimizing CPU memory usage.

*   **Strengths:** Real-time rendering of large-scale scenes ($4^{12}$ resolution); efficient real-time modification (Union/Subtraction); linear data storage simplifies memory management compared to graph-based structures.
It builds on concepts from Virtual Texture and Virtual Geometry, aiming to combine efficient storage with real-time modification capabilities.
The voxelization step relies on the method by Crassin and Green [2012], and the reconstruction step uses a technique similar to Nanite [Karis et al. 2021].
